title: A Minimum Variance Path Principle for Accurate and Stable Score-Based Density Ratio Estimation
claim: Interpolation path choice changes estimates because high-variance paths make distribution changes unstable, whereas low-variance paths yield smooth, stable transitions.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; estimate grid, then red-vs-green path contrast
description: The figure has three parts. Panel (a) on the left shows a large dark-purple heatmap of a ground-truth tree-like, branching density. Beside it is a 2x2 grid of smaller heatmaps, labeled (i) Linear, (ii) Föllmer, (iii) trigonometric and (iv) VP. Each is a blurrier or distorted version of the truth, which shows that estimates vary with the path setting. Panels (b) and (c) are conceptual cartoons. Each draws a blue dotted teardrop p0 on the left and an orange dotted leaf-shaped blob p1 on the right. Between them are circles of blue and orange dots, labeled p_t, that show the mixture changing. In (b) a wiggly black path is paired with a red arrow and the bold red text 'Path Variance is LARGE', described as dramatic and unstable. In (c) a smooth black path is paired with a green arrow and the green text 'Path Variance is SMALL', described as smooth and stable.
caption: (a) Preliminary experiments under various path settings. The left image denotes the ground truth. (b-c) Probability paths between p0 and p1 with large and small variance, respectively.
abstract: Score-based methods are powerful across machine learning, but they face a paradox: theoretically path-independent, yet practically path-dependent. We resolve this by proving that practical training objectives differ from the ideal, ground-truth objective by a crucial, overlooked term: the path variance of the score function. We propose the MVP (**M**imum **V**ariance **P**ath) Principle to minimize this path variance. Our key contribution is deriving a closed-form expression for the variance, making optimization tractable. By parameterizing the path with a flexible Kumaraswamy Mixture Model, our method learns data-adaptive, low-variance paths without heuristic manual selection. This principled optimization of the complete objective yields more accurate and stable estimators, establishing new state-of-the-art results on challenging benchmarks and providing a general framework for optimizing score-based interpolation. Our code can be found in https://github.com/Hoemr/OpenDRE.git.
